newsitem.title: USA: Mexico drug bribes said paid "all the way to top".
newsitem.headline: Mexico drug bribes said paid "all the way to top".

text.p: A convicted drug trafficker testified on Tuesday that the Gulf drug cartel based in northern Mexico paid bribes "all the way to the top in Mexico City" for protection.

Juan Antonio Ortiz, once a top lieutentant in the cartel but now locked away in a U.S. prison, said the organization spent vast sums of money on bribes to buy law enforcement complicity in shipping Colombian cocaine to the United States.
He said he believed every law enforcement official in Mexico was corrupt.

"Luis Medrano (another cartel insider) told me, 'don't worry as far as law enforcement, we've got it all under control, all the way to the top,'" said Ortiz, who testified in the civil trial of Mario Ruiz Massieu, a former Mexican deputy attorney general accused of taking money from drug-traffickers and stashing it in a Texas bank.
"Medrano gave me assurances that money was being paid all the way to the top in Mexico City...it was being paid all the way to the Attorney General's office," he said.

Prosecutors are trying to confiscate $9 million in a Ruiz Massieu bank account here on grounds that it is laundered money from drug-traffickers, including Juan Garcia Abrego, the convicted capo of the Gulf Cartel who was on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list before his capture in January 1996. Garcia Abrego, convicted on drug charges here last October, is serving a life sentence without parole in a U.S. prison.
Ortiz admitted he had no direct knowledge of payments the Gulf cartel made to Ruiz Massieu, but had been told "everybody was being paid."
"Even the President of Mexico?" asked Kathy Fleming, a Ruiz Massieu attorney.
"I said everybody," Ortiz responded before quickly backpedaling to say that he knew only about the cartel's links to law enforcement, not politicians.
"There's not a single Mexican law enforcement official that is honest?" Fleming asked.

"It goes with the job, the payments come with the job," said Ortiz, a U.S. citizen arrested in 1993 and sentenced to 70 months in prison after agreeing to cooperate with U.S. prosecutors. He also testified in the Garcia Abrego trial.

Ruiz Massieu attorney Tony Canales said in opening arguments on Monday that his client's account in Texas Commerce Bank was not drug money, but a family fortune placed in the United States for safekeeping.

He said Ruiz Massieu was being pursued by the Mexican and U.S. governments because he accused the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) of trying to block his investigation into the 1994 assassination of his brother, Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, a top PRI official.

But the Mexican government says Ruiz Massieu covered up the alleged involvement of Raul Salinas de Gortari in his brother's murder, then fled to the United States in March 1995 where he was captured for failing to declare he was carrying $46,000 in cash.

Salinas, the brother of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, has been jailed for two years without trial on charges he ordered the assassination of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu and compiled an illicit fortune during his brother's administration.
